policy: A decision must name what was examined and carry conditions re-evaluated on every run. Having a control is not evidence that a requirement is met: no PASS may be inferred from the presence of MFA, RLS, CodeQL, an SBOM or a passing test. Anything without a valid, currently-holding decision stays PENDING and NOT_ASSESSED.

conditions.condition: validation is implemented in code, so a document has something to describe
the security documentation set still defines no input validation rules

decisions.note: Validation is implemented but undocumented. Neither the threat model nor the security policy defines how data items are checked against an expected structure, so there is no stated rule an implementation could be measured against. This condition watches those two documents; a rules document added elsewhere would need this decision revisited.

conditions.condition: the platform combines related data items whose consistency would have to be defined
no document defines the logical or contextual consistency expected of combined data items

decisions.note: The code enforces real cross-entity consistency, but no document states what consistency is expected. An undocumented rule cannot be reviewed, and a reviewer cannot tell an intended rule from an accidental one.

conditions.condition: no document states business logic limits, per-user or global

decisions.note: No documented expectation exists for business logic limits, either per user or across the application. This is the gap that also makes V2.3.2 unverifiable.

conditions.condition: the global validation pipe is installed
endpoints still declare an inline body type the pipe cannot validate

decisions.note: Positive validation against declared constraints exists for the endpoints that declare a DTO, and does not exist at all for the ones that do not. Measured across endpoints rather than across DTO files: 81 endpoints declare @Body() body: { ... } as an inline TypeScript type and 78 declare a DTO class. An inline type erases to Object at runtime, ValidationPipe skips a parameter whose metatype it cannot transform, so for those 81 the global pipe validates nothing. 77 of them sit on POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, across roughly twenty modules including settlement-engine and saga - about half the write surface of the API. Correction: this decision was first recorded PASS. The note said every DTO file carries class-validator constraints and the global pipe applies them, which is literally true and still gave the wrong answer, because it measured the DTO files that exist rather than the endpoints that need one - the same wrong-denominator mistake the SBOM coverage work was built to prevent. The conditions passed because they checked main.ts for useGlobalPipes and whitelist: true; both are present, and neither tells you whether the pipe has anything to act on. Some of the 81 are inert legacy surfaces - legacy-admin-identity-boundary.ts replaces the admin role and organization mutators with functions that throw ServiceUnavailable - so they validate nothing and also do nothing; they are not cited as live examples.

conditions.condition: validation runs in the trusted service layer where it runs at all
a body-accepting endpoint still bypasses it with an inline type

decisions.note: Where validation happens it happens server-side, which is the right place. The requirement asks that the application be DESIGNED to enforce input validation at a trusted service layer, and half of it is not. Measured across endpoints rather than across DTO files: 81 endpoints declare @Body() body: { ... } as an inline TypeScript type and 78 declare a DTO class. An inline type erases to Object at runtime, ValidationPipe skips a parameter whose metatype it cannot transform, so for those 81 the global pipe validates nothing. 77 of them sit on POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, across roughly twenty modules including settlement-engine and saga - about half the write surface of the API. The clearest live instance is the partner webhook registration: POST api/partner/webhooks takes { url, events } as an inline type, nothing validates the url, and partner-api.service.ts stores it as given. Correction: this decision was first recorded PASS. The note said every DTO file carries class-validator constraints and the global pipe applies them, which is literally true and still gave the wrong answer, because it measured the DTO files that exist rather than the endpoints that need one - the same wrong-denominator mistake the SBOM coverage work was built to prevent. The conditions passed because they checked main.ts for useGlobalPipes and whitelist: true; both are present, and neither tells you whether the pipe has anything to act on. Some of the 81 are inert legacy surfaces - legacy-admin-identity-boundary.ts replaces the admin role and organization mutators with functions that throw ServiceUnavailable - so they validate nothing and also do nothing; they are not cited as live examples.

conditions.condition: cross-entity consistency is enforced on at least the lab finalisation command

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment deliberately not claimed. On the lab finalisation command the check is exemplary: the sample must belong to the deal and the tenant, its chain of custody must be complete, the signed evidence must be purpose-bound to that sample, shipment, acceptance, lab and protocol number, and the actor must hold signatory authority at that moment. The other commands in the policy table have not been examined, so the requirement is not claimed as met for the application.

conditions.condition: every command declares the status it may be issued from and the roles that may issue it
the authoritative path rejects a command issued from any other status

decisions.note: Deal actions are declared with an explicit from/to pair, and the PostgreSQL authority path rejects any command whose stored status does not match definition.from - inside the transaction that already holds the advisory lock, so the check cannot be raced. This decision covers that authoritative path. A second, different transition map exists in runtime-core/runtime-state-machine.ts, used only by runtime-core.service.ts; it is not what this PASS rests on.

conditions.condition: there is still no documented limit for an implementation to be measured against

decisions.note: The requirement asks that limits be implemented per the documentation. No documentation of business logic limits exists, so no implementation can be verified against it. This fails on the same gap as V2.1.3 and is recorded separately because closing V2.1.3 alone would not close this one.

conditions.condition: deal commands execute inside the shared transactional context
that context is a database transaction with an explicit isolation level

decisions.note: A deal command runs entirely inside one database transaction opened by RlsTransactionService, so it either completes or leaves no partial state. Isolation is explicit rather than implicit, and serializable transactions carry a bounded retry.

conditions.condition: a per-deal lock is taken before any state is read
the contended rows are read under a row lock

decisions.note: Concurrent commands against one deal serialise on a transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed by the deal id, taken as the first statement in the transaction, and the contended rows are read FOR UPDATE. Two requests cannot both act on the same pre-state.

conditions.condition: high-value money movement exists as a single command
no second-approver requirement guards it
a second-approval control does exist elsewhere, on the authority-granting path
the second-approval policy is still invoked by nothing at runtime

decisions.note: Release of funds is issued by one actor holding one role: the command policy carries BANK_RELEASE_REQUEST with no second-approver requirement, so the high-value money flow this requirement targets is unprotected. Two things are true at once and both are recorded, because stating either alone misleads. A complete second-approval policy does exist - accounting-authority-command.policy.ts forbids self-approval, requires the second approver to be a different person from both actor and target, and requires that person to hold SIGNING_AUTHORITY_MANAGE with MFA verified within 300 seconds. And nothing invokes it: its functions have no caller outside their own modules and tests, which the NO_RUNTIME_CALLER condition on this decision now re-checks on every run. The control exists as code and prevents nothing at runtime, the same shape as the anti-fraud detector under V2.4.2. If a caller ever appears, this condition stops holding and the requirement returns to assessment - which is the right outcome, because a wired policy would change the answer.

conditions.condition: the export controller serves bulk data
it still carries no anti-automation control

decisions.note: Rate limiting exists on authentication and a few deal endpoints, but the endpoints that return bulk data carry none - and those are the ones the requirement names, because they are the exfiltration surface. nginx declares limit_req zones, but that configuration is referenced by no deployment file in the repository, so it cannot be shown to apply.

conditions.condition: rapid-submission detection exists
the authoritative command path does not consult it

decisions.note: Rapid-transition detection exists and scores, but it prevents nothing: it is reachable only through its own controller endpoint, the deal command path never calls it, and a flagged score is logged and persisted rather than refused. Its state is also an in-process Map, so it would not survive more than one instance.

conditions.condition: the metrics and export responses declare their content type
the event stream declares its content type before flushing headers

decisions.note: Stated with its denominator, which is the discipline this programme had to learn twice. The API has exactly seven raw response paths: four res.send, two res.json and one res.write. All four res.send sites set Content-Type immediately before sending; both res.json sites let Express set application/json; the res.write site is the event stream, which sets text/event-stream before flushHeaders. There are no res.end, res.sendFile or pipe-to-response paths. Everything else returns through the Nest serialiser or NextResponse.json, both of which set the header themselves. Seven raw paths, seven declared content types, none unaccounted for.

conditions.condition: the production edge is still Caddy on a single REG.RU virtual server
that host is still the sole production host

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment blocked on evidence this programme cannot gather, for the same reason recorded under V12: the production terminator is Caddy on the REG.RU virtual server and its configuration is not in the repository. infra/nginx/nginx.conf is not the production edge and is not evidence about it. Marking this PASS would assert something unverified and marking it FAIL would assert a defect nobody observed. Specifically unverified: whether the edge redirects HTTP to HTTPS and whether it does so only for user-facing endpoints. Credited without letting it answer the question: the API itself sets Strict-Transport-Security in code, which is in the repository and does apply, but a response header instructing future requests is not the same control as a redirect.

conditions.condition: a trusted-proxy policy decides which forwarded value to believe
a global guard consumes that policy rather than reading the header directly

decisions.note: A header set by an intermediary cannot be forged by the client. trusted-proxy.ts parses CIDR ranges for v4 and v6, bounds the forwarded header at 4096 bytes and 20 hops, and resolves the client address by walking the chain against trusted ranges rather than taking the first value. The policy is not decorative: both rate-limit guards call resolveRequestIp, and both are registered as global APP_GUARDs, so it runs on every request. Checked for the failure mode this programme keeps finding - a control with no caller - and it does not apply here.

conditions.condition: CORS is configured
no method allowlist constrains it

decisions.note: No explicit HTTP method allowlist exists. enableCors is configured with an origin and credentials but no methods option, so preflight advertises the framework default rather than the methods this API supports. Credited: route binding means an undeclared method on a declared path does not execute a handler. That limits what runs; it is not the explicit allowlist the requirement asks for, and it says nothing about what preflight advertises.

conditions.condition: at least one sensitive transaction requires a purpose-bound signature beyond transport

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment deliberately not claimed, on the same reasoning as V2.2.3. The lab protocol finalisation does exactly what this requirement describes: it requires a signed evidence reference and validates that the signature is purpose-bound to that sample, shipment, acceptance, laboratory and protocol number - assurance that does not depend on the transport. Whether the other sensitive transactions carry an equivalent per-message signature has not been examined, so the requirement is not claimed as met for the application.

conditions.condition: the production edge is still Caddy on a single REG.RU virtual server
that host is still the sole production host

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment blocked on evidence this programme cannot gather, for the same reason recorded under V12: the production terminator is Caddy on the REG.RU virtual server and its configuration is not in the repository. infra/nginx/nginx.conf is not the production edge and is not evidence about it. Marking this PASS would assert something unverified and marking it FAIL would assert a defect nobody observed. Specifically unverified: whether every component in the chain determines message boundaries the same way. Request smuggling is decided between the edge and the application server, and only one of those two is in the repository.

conditions.condition: the production edge is still Caddy on a single REG.RU virtual server
that host is still the sole production host

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment blocked on evidence this programme cannot gather, for the same reason recorded under V12: the production terminator is Caddy on the REG.RU virtual server and its configuration is not in the repository. infra/nginx/nginx.conf is not the production edge and is not evidence about it. Marking this PASS would assert something unverified and marking it FAIL would assert a defect nobody observed. Specifically unverified: whether a generated Content-Length can disagree with the body as it leaves the edge.

conditions.condition: the production edge is still Caddy on a single REG.RU virtual server
that host is still the sole production host

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment blocked on evidence this programme cannot gather, for the same reason recorded under V12: the production terminator is Caddy on the REG.RU virtual server and its configuration is not in the repository. infra/nginx/nginx.conf is not the production edge and is not evidence about it. Marking this PASS would assert something unverified and marking it FAIL would assert a defect nobody observed. Specifically unverified: whether connection-specific header fields are accepted or emitted over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, which is decided by the terminator.

conditions.condition: the production edge is still Caddy on a single REG.RU virtual server
that host is still the sole production host

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment blocked on evidence this programme cannot gather, for the same reason recorded under V12: the production terminator is Caddy on the REG.RU virtual server and its configuration is not in the repository. infra/nginx/nginx.conf is not the production edge and is not evidence about it. Marking this PASS would assert something unverified and marking it FAIL would assert a defect nobody observed. Specifically unverified: whether header fields containing invalid characters are rejected at the HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 layer.

conditions.condition: a consumer-supplied url is accepted with an inline body type nothing validates
and fetched server-side with no target validation

decisions.note: The application builds and sends requests to an address a consumer chooses, and validates nothing about it. POST api/partner/webhooks takes { url, events } as an inline TypeScript type - so the global validation pipe has no class to act on, per the correction recorded under V2.2.1 - the service stores the url as given, and the dispatcher fetches it server-side. There is no scheme check, no private-address block, no allowlist and no redirect limit, and the tree contains no SSRF protection of any kind. An authenticated partner can point a webhook at an internal service or a cloud metadata endpoint and have the API fetch it on their behalf. Authenticated, and real.

conditions.condition: no GraphQL or data-layer query API is served by the application

decisions.note: The application exposes no GraphQL or equivalent data-layer query API, so there is no query whose depth, amount or cost could need limiting. The one graphql string in the tree is in a test asserting on GitHub CI check data, which is why this condition excludes tests: a reference in a test is not a served API. If one is ever introduced, the condition stops holding and the requirement returns to assessment.

conditions.condition: no GraphQL schema is served, so there is no introspection to disable

decisions.note: No GraphQL API is served, so introspection cannot be enabled or disabled. Recorded separately from V4.3.1 because the two would need different evidence if a GraphQL API were introduced.

conditions.condition: no WebSocket gateway is served by the application
and the client that would dial one is imported by nothing

decisions.note: No WebSocket connection is ever established, so there is no connection whose transport could be required to use TLS. This needs saying carefully, because the surface looks alive: apps/web/lib/websocket-client.ts exists, defaults to ws://localhost:4000, and socket.io is declared in both manifests. But there is no WebSocketGateway, no IoAdapter and no adapter registration anywhere in the API - the server the client comment refers to does not exist - and the client itself is imported by nothing. Recording a FAIL on that ws:// default would describe a defect that cannot occur. Worth stating for the owner rather than the matrix: if a gateway is ever added, it will inherit this client default and its absent origin check, and both conditions here will stop holding at that moment.

conditions.condition: no WebSocket handshake is served, so there is no Origin to check

decisions.note: There is no WebSocket handshake to validate an Origin against, because no gateway is served. The absent origin check in the orphaned client is noted under V4.4.1 as a forward risk rather than a present defect.

conditions.condition: no WebSocket session exists to need a dedicated token

decisions.note: No WebSocket session exists, so the question of whether standard session management can be used there does not arise. The platform session mechanism assessed under V7 covers every connection the application actually makes.

conditions.condition: no dedicated WebSocket token is issued or validated

decisions.note: No dedicated WebSocket session token is obtained or validated anywhere, because no WebSocket session exists to hold one.

conditions.condition: the upload route still carries no reference to a documented upload policy
the upload route is the surface the missing documentation would have to cover

decisions.note: No document defines the permitted file types, expected extensions or maximum size for this upload feature. Unpacked size is the sharpest gap: it is stated nowhere, and decompression itself is uncapped (see V5.2.3). Stated precisely, because the first version of this note said unpacked size was "neither stated nor bounded anywhere" and that was too broad: extracted text is truncated at MAX_EXTRACTED_CHARS and OCR output is bounded by the execFile maxBuffer. Those bound what is kept, not what is inflated, so the requirement still fails - but the note should not suggest that nothing limits anything.

conditions.condition: the size caps exist and are applied in the handler
no ceiling is applied before the body is buffered

decisions.note: The caps (4 files, 8 MiB per file, 24 MiB total) are enforced only after request.formData() has buffered the entire body. The single pre-buffer check trusts a client-supplied Content-Length and is skipped when that header is absent, so an oversized body is read into memory before it is rejected. nginx sets client_max_body_size 10m, but that is an infrastructure ceiling whose deployment cannot be verified from the repository.

conditions.condition: dispatch is driven by the filename extension
no content-based file type detection is performed

decisions.note: Processing is selected purely from the filename extension. Nothing inspects the file signature, and the reported mediaType is echoed from the client-controlled file.type. A file may declare any extension its content does not match.

conditions.condition: the route decompresses archive and stream content
no ceiling is placed on decompressed output

decisions.note: inflateRawSync (docx member) and inflateSync (PDF FlateDecode streams) are called without maxOutputLength, and no cap on the number of archive entries exists. A compression bomb inside word/document.xml or a PDF stream inflates without a ceiling inside the request handler.

conditions.condition: only per-request caps exist
no per-user quota or stored-file accounting exists

decisions.note: The route enforces per-request limits only. There is no per-user file-count or storage quota, and no accounting that would let one be enforced.

conditions.condition: archive members are read into memory by exact name, never written out
no archive extraction to disk exists that a symlink member could target

decisions.note: No archive member is ever written to the filesystem. zipEntry locates one member by exact name and returns its bytes, so an archive cannot introduce a symlink.

conditions.condition: uploaded images are passed to an image pipeline
no pixel-dimension limit is applied

decisions.note: Uploaded images go straight to normalisation and OCR with no maximum pixel dimension. The 30 s OCR timeout limits the damage but is not the control this requirement asks for.

conditions.condition: working files are written only to a private temporary directory
no uploaded content is written into a web-served directory

decisions.note: Uploaded content is never stored in a public folder. Working files live in a per-request mkdtemp directory under the OS temp path, are written with mode 0600 and removed afterwards, so nothing uploaded is reachable as a server-side program or a static asset.

conditions.condition: every on-disk path is internally generated
the submitted filename is never used to build a path

decisions.note: File paths are built from internally generated names inside a random temporary directory. The submitted filename is retained only as a truncated display label and is never used to construct a path.

conditions.condition: decompression targets one member matched by exact name
no archive-supplied path is joined onto a filesystem path

decisions.note: Path information carried inside an archive is never used. The single member is matched by an exact literal name and its bytes are kept in memory, so zip slip has no route to the filesystem.

conditions.condition: a user-supplied route parameter is still interpolated into a download filename
the parameter is still unvalidated at the controller

decisions.note: exportLedger interpolates the raw @Param('dealId') into the Content-Disposition filename. The parameter is a bare string, so neither ParseUUIDPipe nor the global ValidationPipe constrains it, and the application neither validates nor ignores the user-submitted component.

conditions.condition: download filenames are still emitted as a bare quoted string
no RFC 6266 encoding is applied

decisions.note: Content-Disposition is built as a bare quoted string with no RFC 6266 encoding and no sanitisation of the interpolated value. A quote in dealId breaks the quoted-string. Node refuses CR and LF in header values, so header injection is blocked by the platform rather than by the application.

conditions.condition: the route accepts files from untrusted sources
no antivirus integration exists anywhere in application or package source

decisions.note: Files accepted from untrusted sources are parsed and their text returned with no malware scanning. docs/security/THREAT_MODEL.md already names malware scan and quarantine as a required control; it is not implemented.

conditions.condition: a session lifetime exists in code and would be what a document has to state
no document states an inactivity timeout or a maximum session lifetime

decisions.note: A 30 day absolute lifetime exists in code. No document states it, states an inactivity timeout, or justifies either against risk. An undocumented timeout cannot be reviewed as appropriate, which is what this requirement asks.

conditions.condition: no concurrent-session limit is enforced in the session service
no document defines how many parallel sessions an account may hold

decisions.note: Neither the limit nor its documentation exists. An account may hold unlimited parallel sessions; organization-team.service.ts surfaces an activeSessionCount for display, which counts sessions rather than bounding them.

conditions.condition: the platform participates in a federated identity ecosystem as a relying party
no document covers session management for that federated participation

decisions.note: The platform is an OIDC relying party against a government identity provider, so it is part of a federated identity ecosystem and this requirement applies. No documentation covers how sessions in that ecosystem are created, timed out or terminated.

conditions.condition: both verification paths read the session from the database rather than trusting the token

decisions.note: Session verification is a backend database read on every request, on both paths. The token carries a session id; authority comes from the stored row. A client cannot assert its own session state, and revocation takes effect on the next request rather than at the next refresh. Unlike the two token verifiers assessed under V9, these two session paths agree - auth.service.ts is in fact stricter, adding membership status, organization verification and role validity.

conditions.condition: session and refresh identifiers are generated per authentication

decisions.note: Sessions are represented by dynamically generated reference tokens, not by anything derived from user data. Each authentication mints a fresh session id and a fresh refresh-token family id.

conditions.condition: reference token secrets come from a cryptographic random source
stored values are digests compared in constant time

decisions.note: A reference token is 32 random bytes with an 18 byte random identifier. Only an HKDF-derived digest is stored, and comparison is constant-time, so neither guessing nor a timing oracle nor a database read yields a usable token.

conditions.condition: authentication mints a new session rather than reusing one
the new session is unusable until the second factor completes

decisions.note: Each authentication creates a new session with a new identifier and a new refresh family, and the session starts in MFA_PENDING so the identifier issued before the second factor cannot be used as an authenticated one. Refresh rotates the credential on every use and reuse of a rotated token revokes the entire family.

conditions.condition: an absolute lifetime exists
no inactivity tracking exists to build a timeout on

decisions.note: There is no inactivity timeout, and no last-activity timestamp from which one could be derived. A session left untouched stays valid for its full 30 day absolute lifetime. This is a separate gap from V7.3.2: an absolute cap does not bound idle exposure.

conditions.condition: an absolute maximum lifetime is enforced
no documented limit exists to enforce it against

decisions.note: An absolute maximum is enforced and re-checked on every request, which is the mechanical half of this requirement. It fails on the other half: the requirement asks that the limit follow risk analysis and documentation, and 30 days is stated nowhere and justified nowhere. Recorded as FAIL rather than PASS because an unreviewed number is not a risk decision.

conditions.condition: a terminated session is refused on both paths

decisions.note: Termination is honoured on the next request, not the next token refresh, because both paths re-read session status from the database each time. A revoked or expired session yields no further access even while its access token is still within its 15 minute validity.

conditions.condition: a session belonging to a non-active user is refused
the platform path also refuses on membership and organization state

decisions.note: Disabling an account terminates its sessions in effect: every request re-reads user status and refuses anything that is not ACTIVE, then revokes the session. No separate sweep is needed, so there is no window in which a disabled account still holds a live session. The platform path additionally follows membership and organization state, which covers an employee removed from an organization rather than deactivated outright.

conditions.condition: a successful password change advances the credential version
a session minted under an older credential version is refused

decisions.note: A password change increments the credential version, and both session paths refuse any session whose recorded version no longer matches. Every other session ends immediately. Stated precisely: the application does not offer this as an option, it does it unconditionally, which exceeds what the requirement asks for. No option UI exists and none is claimed.

conditions.condition: a logout control exists in the protected shell
the protected shell renders that control

decisions.note: Under /platform-v7 this is satisfied: the logout control lives in the header menu rendered by the protected shell, which the route-group layout applies to every page beneath it. It fails as a whole because other authenticated surfaces do not sit under that layout - the platform-v7r runtime, the staff plane and the GEKTA product pages have their own shells, and no equivalent control was verified in them. Recorded as FAIL rather than a scoped PASS because the requirement asks about all pages that require authentication, and only one shell was proven.

conditions.condition: an administrator can terminate another user sessions
the staff plane can review and revoke sessions

decisions.note: POST auth/sessions/revoke-user is restricted to ADMIN and terminates every session of the named user. The staff plane additionally offers permission-gated review of all active sessions and revocation of an individual one. The requirement asks for per-user or all-user termination; per-user exists and is enforced by role.

conditions.condition: the role change is implemented in this service
that service still requires no re-authentication for it
a wired fresh-MFA gate does exist elsewhere, so the capability is real

decisions.note: A fresh-MFA gate exists and is genuinely wired: registration-decision.service.ts refuses a review decision unless the reviewer verified MFA within 15 minutes, at three call sites. It is credited here because it shows the capability is real and invoked - unlike the signing-authority policy under V2.3.5, which has no callers at all. But it guards registration review, not account attributes. Changing an organization membership role is a sensitive attribute change and organization-invitation.service.ts applies no re-authentication to it - only rate limiting at the controller and an optimistic version check. The password path is different and defensible: there is no in-session password change endpoint, only a reset requiring an emailed token, which is itself a re-authentication.

conditions.condition: the staff plane lets a caller view and terminate their own sessions
the user-facing auth surface offers no equivalent

decisions.note: Staff can view their active sessions and revoke one. Ordinary platform users cannot: the only session-termination endpoint on the user-facing auth surface is ADMIN-only. The capability constant SECURITY_SESSION_REVOKE_OWN is defined in membership-capability.resolver.ts but is wired to no route, so it grants nothing. The staff plane is credited; the gap is the user plane.

conditions.condition: a highly sensitive money operation exists as a command
the path that executes it still asks for no further authentication
a wired further-authentication gate exists elsewhere, so the capability is real

decisions.note: Releasing funds is the most sensitive operation this platform performs, and the path that executes it asks for nothing beyond an already-authenticated session. The session must carry a verified second factor to exist at all, which is a real baseline, but the requirement asks for further authentication at the point of the operation and there is none: no fresh-MFA check, no step-up, no secondary verification anywhere on the command path. The capability is not missing from the platform - registration-decision.service.ts refuses a decision unless MFA was verified within 15 minutes - it is simply not applied where the money moves. Read together with V2.3.5, the money-release command has neither a second approver nor a re-authentication step.

conditions.condition: the platform acts as a relying party against an external identity provider
no session termination is propagated between relying party and provider

decisions.note: The platform is a relying party: it builds an authorization-code request with client_id, redirect_uri, scope openid, state and nonce. Nothing propagates session termination in either direction - no RP-initiated logout, no front-channel or back-channel logout, no logout_token handling - and no document describes what the behaviour should be. Both halves of the requirement are unmet.

conditions.condition: the federated flow is started by an explicit user action carrying anti-forgery state
the flow is disabled unless deliberately configured

decisions.note: A federated session is never created implicitly. The flow begins only from an explicit user action, carries a per-request random state and nonce in httpOnly SameSite=Lax cookies with a ten minute lifetime, and is inert entirely unless the bridge is configured and enabled. A drive-by request cannot mint a session.

conditions.condition: function and data level restrictions are enforced in code and policy
no document defines the rules those restrictions implement

decisions.note: The restrictions themselves are strong and enforced in the database. What is missing is the statement of what they are meant to be: no document defines function-level or data-specific access rules, so an implementation cannot be reviewed against an intent. This is the same shape of gap as V2.1.x and V7.1.x, and it is the one place this otherwise strong chapter is consistently weak.

conditions.condition: no document defines field-level read or write restrictions

decisions.note: No document defines which consumer may read or write which field. Recorded separately from V8.2.3 because one is the missing rule and the other is the missing control; closing either alone would not close the other.

conditions.condition: no document defines environmental or contextual attributes for access decisions

decisions.note: No document defines time, location, device or any other contextual attribute as an input to access decisions. Consistent with V8.2.4, where no such control exists to document.

conditions.condition: no document describes how contextual factors enter authorization decisions

decisions.note: Nothing describes how environmental or contextual factors would be weighed, because none are used. The requirement is unmet rather than inapplicable: the platform makes access decisions, it simply makes them without these inputs and without saying so.

conditions.condition: authentication is a global guard rather than a per-route opt-in
the guard refuses a request without a bearer token
the public escape hatch is refused for sensitive flags in production

decisions.note: Function-level access is deny by default: AppAuthGuard is registered as a global APP_GUARD, so every route requires an authenticated consumer unless explicitly marked public. What makes that real rather than nominal is the second half - the public escape is itself gated by an environment flag, and the guard refuses the sensitive public flags outright in production. A route cannot be opened up in production by flipping a variable. 45 of 54 controllers carry role or guard decorators on top of this.

conditions.condition: row policies decide on the bound subject where they exist
a tenant-bearing table still carries no row level security

decisions.note: Where a policy exists, data-specific access is decided per row by PostgreSQL from the authenticated subject, and that part is strong. It is not universal. Measured denominator: 40 Prisma models carry tenantId, 37 map to a table with ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and 3 have no policy at all - deal_events, fgis_grain_tenant_read_provider_claims and fgis_grain_tenant_read_audit_heads. The two FGIS tables look missed rather than excluded: the same migration enables row level security on fgis_grain_tenant_read_authorizations and fgis_grain_tenant_read_audits. Stated precisely in both directions. deal_events is live - the authoritative command path reads and writes it inside the RLS transaction - but with no policy on the table the transaction-local tenant setting constrains nothing there. No cross-tenant read is exposed today: the one service that would read it filtered by dealId alone, DealEventService, has no reference outside its own file and is registered in no module. So this is a missing control, not an observed breach. deal_events is not unprotected either - the industrial transaction core migration enforces append-only on it - but append-only is an integrity control, not a tenancy control, and says nothing about which tenant may read the rows. Also not a finding: the 165 plain-client Prisma calls against 146 transaction-wrapped ones. On a table that HAS a policy, a read outside the transaction has no tenant setting, the policy cannot match, and the read returns nothing - fail-closed, the correct direction. Correction: this decision was first recorded PASS on 72 tables with row level security and 268 policies. Those numbers are real and they were the wrong measurement: they count the tables that have the control, not the tables that need it. I flagged that denominator as unverified when reporting the chapter and then verified it, which is what turned the verdict.

conditions.condition: the access control that exists operates on rows
no field-level restriction exists alongside it

decisions.note: This is the requirement most at risk of being answered with the wrong evidence, so it is stated plainly: row level security restricts WHICH ROWS a consumer sees. It says nothing about WHICH FIELDS of a row they may read or write. No column-level grants, no field allowlists, no per-field write restrictions exist anywhere. The strength of the row-level control does not carry over, and treating it as though it did would be exactly the inference this mechanism exists to prevent.

conditions.condition: no adaptive control reads time, location or device as an access input

decisions.note: No adaptive or contextual security control exists. The only geolocation reference in the application is a Permissions-Policy header that disables it. The requirement is unmet, not inapplicable - an application making authorization decisions could use these inputs and this one does not.

conditions.condition: authorization is enforced by a server-side global guard
and again below the service layer, in the database
the database layer does not yet cover every tenant-bearing table

decisions.note: Enforcement sits in two places a client cannot reach: a global server-side guard, and row policies inside PostgreSQL. Nothing an untrusted consumer controls participates in the decision, and that holds for this requirement, which asks that the rules be enforced at a trusted service layer rather than that the database cover everything. Wording corrected: the first version said the database layer "holds even if the service layer forgets". That is true for the 37 tenant-bearing tables with a policy and false for the 3 without, so the claim is now scoped rather than universal. The trusted-layer requirement is still met - the guard is global and the policies are real - while the coverage gap is recorded where it belongs, under V8.2.2 and V8.4.1.

conditions.condition: the access token carries no authorization value that could go stale
authorization values are read from the session row on each request

decisions.note: Changes apply immediately because there is nothing cached to apply them to. The access token carries only a type, a session id, a credential version and a subject - no role, no tenant, no capability. Every request re-reads role, membership status and organization status from the database. A role change or a membership deactivation takes effect on the next request, so the requirement never reaches its own fallback clause about changes that cannot be applied immediately. The condition here checks the absence of authorization claims in the token rather than asserting immediacy, because that absence is what makes immediacy structural rather than incidental.

conditions.condition: the originating subject is what the database sees
acting on a client behalf is explicitly refused, not merely absent
that refusal is wired into the regulatory path

decisions.note: Access decisions are made on the originating consumer identity: the transaction binds their user id and the policies read it, and no service account, impersonation or run-as construct exists anywhere to substitute a different subject. The sharper evidence is not the absence but the refusal - the platform implements denyLegacyFgisActionOnBehalfOfClient for a legally significant action it must never perform for a client, and calls it from four places in the regulatory path. An intermediary is not merely unimplemented; it is rejected.

conditions.condition: tenant identity is bound transaction-locally before any work runs
a tenant-bearing table still carries no row level security

decisions.note: The requirement says a consumer operation must NEVER affect a tenant they have no relationship with. "Never" is not established. Measured denominator: 40 Prisma models carry tenantId, 37 map to a table with ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and 3 have no policy at all - deal_events, fgis_grain_tenant_read_provider_claims and fgis_grain_tenant_read_audit_heads. The two FGIS tables look missed rather than excluded: the same migration enables row level security on fgis_grain_tenant_read_authorizations and fgis_grain_tenant_read_audits. For those three tables there is no boundary below the service layer, which is exactly what the first version of this note claimed as its strength. Stated precisely in both directions. deal_events is live - the authoritative command path reads and writes it inside the RLS transaction - but with no policy on the table the transaction-local tenant setting constrains nothing there. No cross-tenant read is exposed today: the one service that would read it filtered by dealId alone, DealEventService, has no reference outside its own file and is registered in no module. So this is a missing control, not an observed breach. deal_events is not unprotected either - the industrial transaction core migration enforces append-only on it - but append-only is an integrity control, not a tenancy control, and says nothing about which tenant may read the rows. Also not a finding: the 165 plain-client Prisma calls against 146 transaction-wrapped ones. On a table that HAS a policy, a read outside the transaction has no tenant setting, the policy cannot match, and the read returns nothing - fail-closed, the correct direction. Correction: this decision was first recorded PASS on 72 tables with row level security and 268 policies. Those numbers are real and they were the wrong measurement: they count the tables that have the control, not the tables that need it. I flagged that denominator as unverified when reporting the chapter and then verified it, which is what turned the verdict.

conditions.condition: the administrative guard requires an active time-bound staff session
and refuses a session that does not match the actor
administrative endpoints require a named permission and an access mode

decisions.note: An administrative call passes four independent layers: the global authentication guard, a staff access guard requiring an active time-bound session bound to the actor, an access-mode check, and a named permission. The identity half of the requirement is continuous rather than established once: the staff session is re-verified on every request and expires on its own clock, and a session header that does not match the acting identity is refused.

conditions.condition: the API verifier checks the signature before reading any claim
the web verifier returns the payload only after the MAC verifies

decisions.note: Both token verifiers in the tree check the signature or MAC before any claim is read. The web verifier decodes the payload only after crypto.subtle.verify returns true; the API verifier reads claims only from the value jwt.verify returned.

conditions.condition: the API verifier still states no algorithm allowlist
the web verifier does state one

decisions.note: The two verifiers disagree. The web verifier rejects any header whose alg is not HS256 before verifying - that is the allowlist the requirement asks for. The API verifier passes no algorithms option to jwt.verify. jsonwebtoken 9 refuses alg none and, given a string secret, restricts itself to HMAC, so the protection is real - but it comes from a library default rather than from a stated allowlist, and a future dependency change or a switch to a key object would move it silently. The requirement asks for the allowlist to be stated.

conditions.condition: the API key material comes from a required pre-configured secret
no verifier resolves key material from a token-supplied source

decisions.note: Validation keys come from configuration, not from the token. There is no JWKS endpoint, no remote key set and no kid-directed key lookup anywhere, so a token cannot nominate the key that verifies it.

conditions.condition: the API issues a bounded lifetime and verifies it
the web verifier rejects an expired or not-yet-valid token

decisions.note: Access tokens carry a 15 minute expiry that jwt.verify enforces, and the web verifier checks both exp and nbf against the supplied time. A token outside its validity span is refused by both paths.

conditions.condition: the API verifier does check the token type
the web verifier still checks neither type nor audience
the cabinet session route signs and verifies with the API token secret

decisions.note: The API verifier does this correctly: it rejects a token whose typ is not access. The web verifier does not check type at all, and the cabinet session route hands it process.env.JWT_SECRET - the same secret the API signs access tokens with. So any HS256 token signed with that secret verifies there regardless of what it was issued for. In practice an access token yields no cabinet role because it carries no role claim, but that is a behavioural accident, not a type check. The staff route is not part of this gap: it does check purpose-bearing claims (owner, testAccess, sub, email) after verifying.

conditions.condition: the API verifier does constrain the audience
the web verifier still applies no audience restriction

decisions.note: The API verifier passes an audience to jwt.verify, so a token minted for another audience is refused there. The web verifier applies no audience restriction, so it accepts tokens not intended for it. One of the two services meets the requirement; the requirement is about the service receiving the token, and one of them does not.

conditions.condition: issued access tokens carry an audience restriction

decisions.note: One private key is used to issue tokens for more than one consumer - the API access token and the web cabinet session token share JWT_SECRET - which is exactly the situation this requirement addresses. Issued access tokens do carry an audience restriction, so the token itself states who it is for. Whether every receiver enforces that restriction is a separate matter, and it is recorded as failing under V9.2.3.

conditions.condition: the document most likely to be mistaken for a key management policy still exists and is still an exposure report
no document in the security set defines a key lifecycle
the approved data classification exists and gives the key policy something to protect

decisions.note: There is no key management policy. docs/security/SECRET_ROTATION_REGISTER.md is named so that a reader will reach for it here, so it is named explicitly: it is a secret-exposure scan report plus an incident procedure for what to do when a credential is found in Git. It defines no crypto-period, no custody rule, no limit on how many entities may hold a shared secret, and no alignment to a key management standard. Its own closing line says the inventory for material held outside Git "does not exist yet". The gap is the policy, not the capability - two subsystems already implement real key replacement (versioned outbox keys, bank keys with overlapping windows and database-backed revocation), and they do it without a written rule to implement. What that rule should say is an owner decision. Update: the owner has since approved a canonical data classification, which supplies the policy basis this requirement was missing on one side - C11_CRYPTO_SECRET now names what counts as key material and states that it is never logged, never sent to analytics, telemetry or an external model, and never carried in a query string. That is handling, not lifecycle. This requirement additionally asks for a key management standard, a crypto-period per key and a limit on how many entities may hold a shared secret, and none of those is decided. The verdict therefore does not change, and the remaining gap is now smaller and precisely stated rather than open-ended.

conditions.condition: no cryptographic inventory exists in the security documentation set
the supply-chain artefact that is adjacent to this requirement still exists and still is not this
the mechanical inventory of algorithms and key names exists
the data side of the mapping exists, so what is missing is the link between the two

decisions.note: No cryptographic inventory exists. The SBOM work already merged is adjacent and must not be offered as if it answered this: an SBOM enumerates components, while this requirement asks for keys, algorithms and certificates, where each key may and may not be used, and which data each key may protect. Nothing in the repository states any of that. The material for one is now measurable - one cipher (AES-256-GCM, 15 sites), one hash (SHA-256), one MAC (HMAC-SHA256), one KDF (HKDF-SHA256), one password function (bcrypt), and roughly eleven distinct key-holding subsystems - but a measurement taken once during an assessment is not a maintained inventory, and this decision does not pretend otherwise. Update: two of the three pieces this requirement asks for now exist and are maintained. The algorithm and key-name inventory is generated by a repository-owned mechanism and guarded against going stale (V11.1.3), and the approved data classification defines the types of data that exist and how each class must be handled. What is still missing is the link between them - which key may protect which class of data, and where each key may and may not be used. That mapping is partly derivable from code and partly a decision: which keys a given subsystem is permitted to use is not observable from the fact that it currently uses them. The verdict stands, with the gap reduced to that single named artefact.

conditions.condition: the discovery mechanism still exists and still emits a versioned inventory
the generated inventory is still committed rather than produced and discarded
the guard that fails when the committed inventory goes stale is still present
CI still runs when the mechanism or its artefact changes

decisions.note: A repository-owned discovery mechanism now enumerates every instance of cryptography rather than reporting only the instances a security suite dislikes. It scans 2127 non-test source files under apps and packages, excluding apps/landing, and records encryption, decryption, hashing, MAC, three key-derivation families, password hashing, signature generation and verification, key-pair generation, key exchange, CSPRNG, UUID and non-CSPRNG randomness, constant-time comparison and WebCrypto - each with the algorithm, the call count and the files, and each reported as zero rather than omitted when absent. Key material is named and never read; a test asserts no key value can reach the artefact. Names that match the pattern but configure key material rather than being it - a keyring directory, a current-version pointer, a token budget - are labelled configuration rather than silently dropped, because discarding a match makes a list look cleaner than it is. The mechanism is employed rather than merely available: the artefact is committed, CI runs the scanner whenever it or its inputs change, and a test fails when the committed inventory no longer matches what the scanner produces, so it cannot rot into a one-off snapshot. The first run earned its keep immediately by finding two HMAC-SHA1 sites that the manual sweep behind this chapter had missed; see V11.4.1, whose note is corrected accordingly.

conditions.condition: no migration path to new cryptographic standards is documented
the primitives with the largest post-quantum exposure are still absent from the application

decisions.note: No inventory (V11.1.2) and no migration plan. Two facts make this cheaper to fix than it looks, and neither is a substitute for the plan. The algorithm set is uniform, so a migration would have one cipher, one hash and one KDF to move rather than a spread. And the application performs no asymmetric cryptography at all - the condition scans 3442 source files for key-pair generation and Diffie-Hellman and finds none - so the classic quantum exposure, key exchange and public-key signatures, is currently carried entirely by TLS at the edge rather than by this code. That is a property of today tree, not a documented reaction to a future threat, which is what the requirement asks for.

conditions.condition: the hand-written JWT verifier still delegates the primitive to WebCrypto rather than implementing it
no re-implementation of cryptographic primitives is declared as a dependency

decisions.note: Every cryptographic primitive comes from node:crypto (OpenSSL), WebCrypto, or a published library - bcryptjs 2.4.3 and jsonwebtoken 9.0.3, both pinned in the lockfile. No primitive is re-implemented in the repository, and the eight manifests declare no JavaScript re-implementation of one. The one place that could be mistaken for hand-rolled cryptography is named rather than omitted: apps/web/lib/platform-v7/verified-session.ts parses and checks an HS256 JWT by hand instead of using a library. What is hand-written there is the envelope handling; the HMAC-SHA256 itself is crypto.subtle. Hand-written envelope parsing carries its own risks, which belong to V9, and this decision makes no claim about them.

conditions.condition: key replacement is implemented in the one subsystem that has it
the MFA envelope still rejects every key version but its own, so its version label is not a rotation path

decisions.note: Agility is real in two places and absent everywhere else, so the denominator matters. Key replacement: the auth-mail outbox holds versioned key files and derives per-version keys, and the bank callback registry accepts several keys at once with validity windows plus immediate database-backed revocation - those two can be rotated without downtime. The remaining key-holding subsystems hold one unversioned value each, so replacing the key invalidates every token or ciphertext already issued under it. auth-crypto is the case worth naming precisely: it stamps a v1 label into every MFA ciphertext and then rejects any other version on decrypt, so the label reserves a rotation path rather than providing one. Algorithm replacement: aes-256-gcm appears as a string literal at 15 call sites and sha256 at 95, none of them configurable, so changing a cipher or a hash means editing every site. Re-encryption of stored data has no mechanism outside the auth-mail outbox.

conditions.condition: the 32-character floor for configured secrets is still enforced and still fails closed in production
no cipher below 256-bit key length and no deprecated cipher is present

decisions.note: Every primitive clears 128 bits. AES-256-GCM is the only cipher present; SHA-256 is the only hash used cryptographically; HMAC-SHA256 and HKDF-SHA256 produce 32-byte outputs. Configured key material is floored at 32 characters by a central resolver that refuses to start a production process when a secret is missing or short, and the phone encryption key must decode to exactly 32 bytes or the service throws. No asymmetric key exists anywhere in the application, so the key-size question that this requirement illustrates with RSA and ECC does not arise here; that absence is machine-checked by the V11.1.4 and V11.6.1 conditions rather than assumed.

conditions.condition: one module still owns the bcrypt cost for the whole platform
both login paths still route the comparison through that module rather than choosing a fallback themselves
no file outside the owning module and the seed calls bcrypt hashing at all, so none can pick its own cost
the test that fails if the dummy and the stored cost diverge is still present
patterns: generates the dummy hash at the same cost as a stored password

decisions.note: Comparison of secrets is constant-time and the two login branches now do the same work. All 20 timingSafeEqual sites check length first or catch the length exception, which is the failure this pattern usually has. The work-factor gap recorded when this chapter was first assessed is closed at its cause rather than at its symptom: the cost was previously a literal in four writers plus two dummy-hash sites, and those drifted apart until the unknown-account dummy stood at bcrypt cost 10 against stored passwords at cost 12 - roughly a quarter of the work, so response time reported whether an email was registered. One module now declares the cost, derives the dummy from that same constant, and owns the branch itself: verifyPassword always performs exactly one comparison, against the stored hash when the account exists and against the dummy when it does not, so a future login path cannot skip bcrypt for a missing user or reach for a dummy of another cost. The conditions watch both login paths, the single declaration, the absence of any other caller of bcrypt hashing, and the test that fails if the two costs ever diverge again. One residue is stated rather than hidden: rows hashed before this change at some other cost keep that cost until their owner next sets a password, so existing accounts can still differ from each other. That is inherent to bcrypt without rehash-on-login and is a separate decision; what this requirement asks about - an artificial difference between the known and unknown branches - is gone.

conditions.condition: no padded block mode exists, so the padding-oracle class cannot arise
every decryption path still authenticates before returning plaintext

decisions.note: All six modules that decrypt use AES-GCM, and all six set the authentication tag before reading plaintext, so a modified ciphertext fails at final() and no plaintext is produced. There is no padded block mode anywhere in 3442 source files, so the padding-oracle class is structurally absent rather than merely unexploited. One asymmetry is named rather than smoothed over: decryptMfaSecret throws a distinguishable error for a malformed envelope and lets the GCM failure propagate separately, which would be an oracle if a caller could supply the ciphertext. It cannot - the value is read from the credential row in the database at both call sites - so the distinction is not reachable by an attacker. Every other decrypt path returns null for both cases.

conditions.condition: no insecure block mode is present in the tree
the approved mode is still the one in use at every cipher site

decisions.note: Every cipher instantiation in the repository is AES-256-GCM: 15 occurrences of the algorithm string across six modules, and no other algorithm string anywhere. GCM is an unpadded counter mode, so the weak-padding half of this requirement has nothing to attach to, and PKCS#1 v1.5 in particular cannot arise because no RSA operation exists. The denominator here is every createCipheriv and createDecipheriv call, not a sample: the two calls were enumerated first and each was read.

conditions.condition: AES-GCM is still the algorithm at every cipher site
no unapproved cipher has been introduced
no re-implementation of a cipher is declared as a dependency

decisions.note: AES with GCM is the example this requirement gives, and it is the only cipher the application has. The 1616 apparent matches for "des" in an earlier sweep were substring noise inside words such as "described" and "designed"; re-run with the algorithm string rather than the three letters, the count is zero. Nothing in the eight manifests provides a second cipher implementation that could be reached without a createCipheriv call.

conditions.condition: every encryption site still produces an authentication tag
every decryption site still requires that tag

decisions.note: Encrypted data is protected by an approved authenticated encryption method rather than by a separate MAC. Both halves are checked, because either alone would be misleading: all six modules call getAuthTag on encrypt and all six call setAuthTag on decrypt, so a tag is always produced and always required. Two of them go further and bind context that is not part of the ciphertext - the auth-mail envelope and the Gekta ticket both pass additional authenticated data - so a valid envelope cannot be replayed into a different purpose.

conditions.condition: every encryption site still draws a fresh 96-bit IV from the CSPRNG
no counter-based or fixed IV construction has been introduced

decisions.note: Each of the seven encryption operations generates its IV with randomBytes at call time, so no IV is reused across a key and data pair. Twelve bytes is the size GCM is specified for, which is the "appropriate for the algorithm" half of the requirement - a random 96-bit nonce is the standard construction for this mode, and none of the sites derives an IV from a counter, a timestamp or the plaintext. The auth-mail envelope additionally rejects any stored IV that is not exactly IV_BYTES long before attempting to decrypt.

conditions.condition: the authenticated mode that makes this ordering structural is still in use
no separate MAC is composed with a raw cipher, which is the case this requirement guards

decisions.note: The ordering is structural rather than chosen. No encryption algorithm is combined with a separate MAC algorithm anywhere; all six modules use GCM, which is AES in counter mode composed with GMAC computed over the ciphertext - that is encrypt-then-MAC by construction, and the mode does not offer the other orderings. This is recorded as a pass rather than as not-applicable because the property the requirement wants is present, not excused: on decrypt the tag is verified before any plaintext is returned, at all six sites.

conditions.condition: no MD5 hashing is performed by application code
the two SQL md5 calls still build a worker lease token and nothing else
the SHA-1 HMAC is still confined to the TOTP construction that specifies it

decisions.note: SHA-256 is the hash for every cryptographic purpose: digests, HMAC, HKDF and content integrity. MD5 is named here rather than left for a reader to find, because grepping the repository for it returns two hits and a silent pass would look like a miss. Both are PostgreSQL md5() calls that build a worker lease token from random() and clock_timestamp(), and both were followed to their use: the token is matched in the UPDATE guard that stops two workers claiming the same row. It is a concurrency token, not a secret, a credential, a signature, a key derivation or a random-bit generator, so it is not a cryptographic use and MD5 collision resistance is irrelevant to it. The single createHash("sha1") in the tree is negative test data inside a CodeQL model test asserting that the model flags it. Correction, found by the cryptographic discovery mechanism added under V11.1.3 rather than by the manual sweep behind this chapter: the claim that SHA-256 is the hash for every cryptographic purpose was incomplete. Two runtime sites use HMAC-SHA1 - the TOTP code generator in auth-crypto and a second RFC 6238 implementation in the MFA service. That is not a defect and the verdict does not change: RFC 6238 specifies HMAC-SHA1 for TOTP, every authenticator application implements it, and HMAC does not rest on the collision resistance that SHA-1 has lost, so HMAC-SHA1 remains approved for this use where bare SHA-1 would not be. It is recorded here because a reader who greps for sha1 will find these two, and an assessment that did not mention them would look like one that missed them - which, until the mechanism ran, it had. That the platform carries two independent TOTP implementations is a separate question and belongs to V6.

conditions.condition: stored passwords are still written with bcrypt at cost 12, declared once
the seed no longer chooses its own weaker cost
the test that fails if the cost drops below the current floor is still present
patterns: keeps the cost at or above the current owasp floor for bcrypt

decisions.note: Every path that stores a user password uses bcrypt at cost 12, and the cost is now declared in one place instead of four. Cost 12 is above the current OWASP floor for bcrypt, so the parameter meets guidance rather than merely being non-zero, and a test asserts that floor so a future reduction fails rather than passing quietly. The distribution that was recorded when this chapter was first assessed is no longer split: the canonical test deal seed previously wrote at cost 10, which left a seeded account distinguishable by the same measurement that V11.2.4 is about, and it now takes the shared constant like every other writer. bcryptjs 2.4.3 remains the implementation; no cryptography was written for this.

conditions.condition: the credential digest is still SHA-256 rather than a shorter hash
no non-test source file uses a hash shorter than 256 bits

decisions.note: Every hash used for data authentication or integrity is SHA-256, which is 256 bits and therefore clears the collision-resistance bar rather than only the second-preimage bar. The uses were followed individually: the raw body digest that pins a regulatory message to its stored projection, the SHA-256 of an API key that is stored in place of the key, and the digest that pins the ASVS source document this matrix is built from. No digital signature exists in the application, so the signature half of this requirement has no instance; that absence is machine-checked under V11.6.1 rather than assumed here. The second condition deliberately excludes test files. The one createHash("sha1") in the repository is an assertion inside a CodeQL model test that the model flags exactly that call, so a tree-wide absence check would contradict a fixture whose whole purpose is to contain the thing being forbidden.

conditions.condition: no user-supplied password reaches any key derivation site
the key material those sites do derive from is still floored at 32 characters

decisions.note: This requirement is scoped to keys derived from passwords, and no such derivation exists. Passwords reach bcrypt for verification and nothing else; the four key derivation sites take configured secrets or key files, floored at 32 characters and fetched from the environment or a key file, never from a login form. Key stretching is therefore the wrong control for these inputs - stretching buys time against guessing a low-entropy secret, and these inputs are not low-entropy. Two of the derivations are named so they are not mistaken for an omission: mfa-login-ticket and auth-crypto derive their key with a single SHA-256 pass rather than HKDF. That is adequate for a high-entropy input but provides no domain separation between purposes, which is recorded as part of the agility gap in V11.2.2 rather than treated as a password-stretching failure here.

conditions.condition: credentials are still generated from the CSPRNG at 256 bits
the demo generator is still refused before it runs in production
the controlled-test generator is still refused before it runs in production

decisions.note: The claim is scoped: every value intended to be non-guessable on a production-reachable path is generated by a CSPRNG with at least 128 bits. Counting Math.random alone would have measured the wrong set, because ASVS 5.0 states that UUIDs do not satisfy the 128-bit condition and randomUUID carries 122. So all three generator classes were enumerated - 47 randomBytes, 306 randomUUID, 50 Math.random - and the latter two were each examined for use as a secret. Exactly two sub-128-bit generators produce a value meant to be unguessable: a CSRF token from Math.random in the demo instant-login route, and a CSRF token from randomUUID in the cabinet lock login. Both sit in handlers that return before reaching that line when NODE_ENV is production, one of them behind a second opt-in flag as well, and the demo route session token beside it is an unsigned literal, so nothing there is a credential in the first place. The remaining Math.random sites are record identifiers, idempotency keys that need uniqueness rather than unpredictability, retry jitter, mock handlers and load-test fixtures. The near-miss is recorded: partner-api.service.ts builds its record id with Math.random on the line after the API key itself, which is randomBytes(32) hex, SHA-256 hashed before storage.

conditions.condition: no user-space pseudo-random generator or entropy pool exists in the tree
no seedable random library is declared as a dependency

decisions.note: The application operates no random number generator of its own. Every non-guessable value comes from node:crypto, which draws from the OpenSSL DRBG seeded by the operating system, and there is no application-level entropy pool, no seeding, no caching of random material and no fallback that would degrade to a weaker source when the CSPRNG is slow - randomBytes throws rather than returning low-quality bytes. That is what makes behaviour under heavy demand a property of the platform rather than of this code, and the conditions check the negative that makes it so: 3442 source files and eight manifests contain no seedable generator that a load-shedding path could fall back to.

conditions.condition: no signature or key-pair operation exists in application code
the one declared signature scheme is still marked unimplemented
the guard that fails the build if signing appears is still in place
the signature verification lifecycle still has no runtime caller

decisions.note: Key generation is randomBytes from the OS CSPRNG - the partner API key is randomBytes(32) rendered as hex - and configured key material is validated for length before use, so no key generation algorithm capable of producing a weak key is involved. No digital signature is generated or verified: a scan of 3442 source files finds no createSign, createVerify or key-pair generation, and three build guards fail if signing appears in the regulatory modules. The one signature scheme the platform declares, GOST R 34.10-2012 with a 256-bit digest for FGIS Grain, carries gostSigningImplemented false in its generated policy. The plumbing that would store a verification verdict is present but inert: recordVerification takes the verdict from its caller rather than computing one, and the condition confirms across 2071 runtime files that nothing calls it. An earlier draft of this note claimed that "verified: true" appears only in a type definition; that was wrong as written, because the string also occurs inside names such as mfaVerified, and the claim now rests on the caller check instead.

conditions.condition: the application still performs no key exchange of its own, so what is unassessed is the edge and only the edge
the transport section that records this blocker is still present

decisions.note: The three internal hops authenticate in three different ways, and only one is sound. Web to API signs each request with HMAC-SHA256 over a version, method, canonical path, timestamp and body hash, deriving the URL from the signed path constant so a signature can never cover a path other than the one dialled. API to Elasticsearch sends HTTP basic auth when ELASTICSEARCH_PASSWORD is set - a shared secret, and by V12.3.3 it travels over plaintext http, so the credential itself is exposed on the wire. That was wrong about Elasticsearch, and the condition that was meant to catch it searched for the wrong words - it looked for "authorization" where the file says "auth:" and "password". Both are fixed here.

decisions.note: No document enumerates what the application talks to over the network, for what purpose, or what happens when a call fails. conditions.condition: the ML service client still sends no authentication header of any kind

decisions.note: Two backend components that do not share the application’s session mechanism are reached without authentication, or with authentication that silently disappears if a variable is unset. The ML scoring client (ml-client.service.ts) sends every request with no Authorization header, no API key, nothing - a scan of the file finds zero occurrences of any credential mechanism. Elasticsearch authentication depends on ELASTICSEARCH_PASSWORD; when unset, auth is undefined and the client connects with none, and nothing fails the startup or the request when that happens, unlike requireSecret() elsewhere in the platform which refuses to start in production without a configured value. The counterexample is worth naming: staff-authority-prisma.service.ts shows what this looks like when done right - a boundary that throws when misconfigured rather than silently degrading.

decisions.note: The staff-access boundary is a real least-privilege control, not an aspiration. STAFF_DATABASE_URL, AUTH_DATABASE_URL, DATABASE_URL and STORAGE_DATABASE_URL are each required to carry a distinct PostgreSQL principal - principalFromUrl() extracts and compares them, and the service throws if the staff principal collides with any other, rather than logging a warning and continuing. A companion inspection query checks the connected principal for superuser, bypass_rls, create_db, create_role and direct runtime-table privileges. Under shouldEnforceDatabasePrincipalBoundary(), a strict acceptance and production path cannot start without a distinct STAFF_DATABASE_URL at all. This is the pattern the rest of V13.2 is measured against, and it is why the other findings in this chapter read as gaps rather than as an unreachable bar.

conditions.condition: the CI-only ephemeral postgres/postgres service-container credential this note relies on as a named counterexample is still present in the workflow file

decisions.note: No default credential exists for service authentication in the deployed application source. A scan of apps/api/src and apps/web/lib for the common default-credential shapes (root/root, admin/admin, postgres/postgres, changeme, a literal "password") returns zero matches. A prior version of this note said the scan covered "application or infrastructure source" and claimed zero matches "anywhere" — that overstated what was checked: a repository-wide review comment correctly pointed out that .github/workflows/*.yml was never scanned, and it is not. Checked in response: 20 workflow files do set POSTGRES_USER: postgres and POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres, all inside a GitHub Actions "services:" block, for example auction-atomic-acceptance.yml. Each of those is an ephemeral service container the runner creates fresh for that one job, bound only to the runner’s own localhost network, and destroyed when the job ends; none of it is present in a deployed image, a Compose file, or any path the production credential resolver reads. This is the standard CI test-fixture idiom, not a default account "present ... before deploying to production," which is the harm this requirement targets, so it does not change the verdict. The central secret resolver requireSecret() is built specifically to make a shipped default impossible in the deployed application: it never returns a literal fallback in production, and in any other environment it generates a random ephemeral value per process rather than a stable guessable one — the rationale comment in the file states this design goal directly.

This is the SSRF-shaped gap this programme has already named informally; V13 gives it a permanent ASVS record. The comparison that makes the gap precise rather than a general impression: ai-assistant.service.ts and restricted-public-qwen.service.ts both check an outbound host against an explicit allowlist (AI_ASSISTANT_ALLOWED_HOSTS, a hardcoded model-host list) before ever calling fetch.
