decisions.note: This requirement asks whether each connection follows its documented configuration - maximum parallel connections, behaviour at the limit, and so on. V13.1.2 and V13.1.3 already establish that no such documentation exists for any service. A connection cannot be shown to follow a configuration that was never written down, so this fails as a direct consequence rather than as an independent finding; closing V13.1.2/V13.1.3 is the precondition for this one ever being assessable as anything but FAIL.

conditions.condition: the Vault Transit client still has no caller outside its own module wiring
the dev-mode stub in the same file is still a reversible non-encryption placeholder

decisions.note: A secrets-management client exists and is not used. VaultTransitService implements encrypt/decrypt through HashiCorp Vault Transit, but a scan of 475 runtime files outside its own module finds no caller - the same "latent, not live" shape the V11 assessment found for a second-approval signing policy. Nothing in the platform is actually secured by a secrets-management solution today; secrets are resolved from environment variables and key files by requireSecret() and the auth-mail keyring, which is a different, narrower thing than a vault that creates, stores, controls access to and destroys backend secrets. The module’s own dev-mode fallback underlines the gap: without VAULT_ADDR set it returns stub:base64(plaintext), which is encoding, not encryption, and would be a serious defect if this path were ever reached from a live caller. It is not reached at all, which is what keeps this a documentation-shaped absence rather than a live vulnerability.

conditions.condition: the secret resolver still takes any name string with no scoping of which caller may resolve which secret

decisions.note: Least privilege for secret access has no code-level mechanism to be measured against. requireSecret(name) is a bare function taking an arbitrary string; any module in the API process can call it with any secret name and receive the value, because the application is a single Node process reading process.env with no capability model layered over it. This is a direct, code-observable fact rather than an infrastructure unknown - unlike host-level questions elsewhere in this programme, no host or edge access is needed to see that nothing here enforces least privilege among callers in the same process. It follows from V13.3.1: a real secrets manager with per-consumer policies (which Vault, unused, would have provided) is the mechanism this requirement is built around, and the platform does not have one in effect.

conditions.condition: the cryptographic inventory still shows encryption and decryption executing in-process rather than through Vault
the isolated module that could carry this work is still uncalled

decisions.note: No cryptographic operation in the platform is performed by an isolated security module. The cryptographic inventory this programme generates and keeps current (V11.1.3) accounts for every encryption, decryption, hashing, MAC and key-derivation call site, and all of them execute via node:crypto inside the application process. The one component that could route this work through an isolated module - Vault Transit - has no runtime caller (V13.3.1), so it protects nothing today. This is a direct consequence of that same absence, not a new instance of it.

conditions.condition: no rotation schedule is documented for any secret, and V13.1.4 already establishes the underlying document does not exist

decisions.note: A secret cannot be configured to expire or rotate per a documented schedule when no schedule is documented (V13.1.4). Two subsystems - the auth-mail outbox and the bank-callback key registry - already support rotation mechanically, accepting multiple key versions with overlapping validity, which is credited under V11.2.2. Neither is driven by a written schedule; both rotate only when an operator manually introduces a new key version. This requirement fails on the absence of the schedule itself, which this decision names as the precondition rather than repeating the mechanical-capability finding already recorded elsewhere.

conditions.condition: the API image build is still multi-stage with a distroless runtime stage that copies only the deployed output, not the build context

decisions.note: Source-control metadata does not reach the deployed image. The build stage does COPY . . and therefore does have .git present, but the runtime stage - the one actually shipped and run - is FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs...:nonroot and copies only /prod/api/ from the build stage via a scoped COPY --from=build, which excludes .git. This was checked carefully rather than assumed: a single-stage Dockerfile with COPY . . would have failed this requirement, and the difference between the two is exactly the multi-stage boundary.

conditions.condition: the bootstrap logger still extends ConsoleLogger with no logLevels restriction, so Nest’s default level set stays active in production
no logLevels restriction exists anywhere in the API source to narrow that default
a runtime call site still logs at debug level with message content, proving the level is live rather than theoretical

decisions.note: Corrected on review: an earlier version of this decision recorded PASS on the reasoning that MaskedLoggerService is not a "verbose or debug" logger, which conflated masking with level suppression — they are different things, and only the first is true here. main.ts does construct the Nest application with new MaskedLoggerService(), and that class does redact sensitive substrings from every log call. But MaskedLoggerService extends ConsoleLogger with no constructor and no logLevels option, so it inherits Nest’s default logger levels, which include debug and verbose; nothing anywhere in apps/api/src sets logLevels or LOG_LEVEL to narrow that default for any environment, including production. This is not a theoretical gap: kafka-producer.service.ts calls this.logger.debug() at two call sites with the Kafka topic and the serialized message value, so debug-level output does execute at runtime whenever the transport-unavailable path is hit, unmasked by anything other than MaskedLoggerService’s substring redaction. Debug/diagnostic log levels are enabled by default, which is exactly what this requirement asks to be verified false. Masking sensitive substrings within debug output is a separate, real control (V16 territory) and does not substitute for the level itself being disabled.

the transport section recording the edge-configuration blocker is still present

decisions.note: Whether directory listings are exposed is a property of the Caddy edge, whose configuration is not under version control. The API itself serves no static files (no express.static call exists in the source), so if this behaviour arises anywhere it arises at the edge, consistent with the same blocker already recorded in V4, V11, V12, V14 and V16.

decisions.note: Whether the HTTP TRACE method is supported in production is decided by the Caddy edge, whose configuration is not in the repository. conditions.condition: the detailed-health endpoint is still labelled internal-only in its own source comment while being publicly reachable
that endpoint still carries no access restriction beyond the blanket @Public() decorator

decisions.note: Corrected on review: an earlier version of this decision read every @Public() decorator in this controller as proof of deliberate, requirement-satisfying public exposure. A review comment correctly pointed out that @Public() only proves authentication was bypassed on purpose; it does not by itself prove the operator intended public exposure, and the code’s own text contradicts that reading for one endpoint. The comment directly above health/detailed reads "Detailed health per ТЗ 13.4 — for internal monitoring only," yet the route is decorated @Public() with no IP allowlist, network-boundary check, or authentication of any kind, and the response body discloses database status, configured integrations, outbox queue depth, and heap usage. That is the requirement’s literal case: technical information disclosure that is not protected, and the "unless explicitly intended" exception cannot be claimed for an endpoint whose own author’s comment says the opposite of "intended for the public." No Swagger/OpenAPI UI is mounted (still true, still checked), and the plain health/ready/metrics/version endpoints are a separate question — metrics and version are each assessed on their own merits elsewhere (V13.4.6 covers version) — but health/detailed alone is enough to fail this requirement as written.

conditions.condition: the unauthenticated version endpoint still returns build date, commit and Node version alongside the version string

decisions.note: A dedicated, explicitly public endpoint returns detailed backend version information with no authentication: GET /version responds with the application version, build date, commit hash and Node.js runtime version. This is precisely what the requirement names - detailed version information of backend components, exposed rather than withheld. Unlike V13.4.5, this requirement carries no "unless explicitly intended" allowance; being deliberate does not satisfy it.

conditions.condition: the transport section recording the edge-configuration blocker is still present

decisions.note: Which file extensions the web tier will serve is Caddy edge configuration, not under version control. Not assessed for the same reason as V4, V11, V12 and V16’s transport requirements.

conditions.condition: the approved classification still exists in machine-readable form
it still records the regulatory level the classification was made against
the policy document still carries the owner approval
the code still mirrors the class list

decisions.note: Sensitive data is identified and classified into protection levels, and the classification takes account of the regulation the platform is subject to. The owner approved twelve canonical classes - C0 public non-personal, C1 internal non-personal, C2 business confidential, C3 basic personal, C4 account and access, C5 identity, C6 financial, C7 operational-by-linkage, C8 special and C9 biometric as prohibited in the current scope, C10 authentication secrets and C11 cryptographic secrets - against a stated 152-ФЗ basis of not below УЗ-2 for the production contour, with special and biometric categories out of scope and prohibited by default, publicly self-disclosed business contacts confined to an isolated public-only contour at УЗ-4, and anonymised aggregates held not to be personal data at all. What makes this a classification rather than a document is that it is binding: the schema is machine-readable, the code mirrors it, and a test fails if the two disagree on the class list, on which classes are redacted outbound or on which may never appear in a query string. The three classifications that previously disagreed - eight value classes in log masking, eleven key names in the assistant minimizer, twenty-two secret names in the cryptographic inventory - are now mapped onto this one, and every field name resolves to exactly one class. Correction: the schema version pattern this condition checked was v1 verbatim, which broke when the retention/database-encryption/integrity pass bumped the schema to v2 - the underlying fact (a machine-readable classification exists) still held, but the condition was pinned tighter than the fact it was meant to verify. Loosened to the version-prefix rather than an exact version, which is what was actually being asserted.

conditions.condition: the document still separates documented requirement from proven enforcement, so completing it cannot be mistaken for enforcing it
every class still carries a closed-items record naming what this decision added, alongside what remains open
the C2 outbound rule the requirement asked for is still bound in code, not only in the document
the enforcement citations this pass added are still checked against the code they cite, so a future rename fails the suite rather than leaving the document wrong

decisions.note: All eight elements this requirement enumerates are now documented per class: general encryption, integrity verification, retention, how data is logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, database-level encryption, privacy technologies via the analytics boundary, and outbound confidentiality including the C2 rule this pass added. This closes the documentation requirement and only the documentation requirement. Two things keep that boundary honest. First, every retention, database-encryption and integrity entry carries a requirement and a separate enforcement statement, and the two disagree in most rows on purpose: retention is documented for every class with a named basis, but enforcement is stated as real only for auth-mail (existing) and lifecycle-bound token TTLs (existing); it is stated as not-enforced for the personal-data classes, because no deletion job exists for them. Database-level encryption is documented as required for C5-C7 and C10-C11, and enforcement is proven true for C10/C11 and for one C3 field (phone), and named false for a specific column - GektaMerchantProfile.inn, plain VarChar, holding a natural person’s INN on НПД/ИП rows - rather than described in general terms. Second, every value grounded in a statute (402-ФЗ Art. 29 for accounting-linked retention, 152-ФЗ Art. 5(7) otherwise) is labelled a proposed default pending confirmation, not a certified legal position; the owner approved the classification and delegated completing this policy, and a specific retention window is this decision’s technical implementation of that delegation, not a new legal conclusion asserted on the owner’s behalf. Enforcement-focused requirements - V14.2.7 for retention, and the database-encryption gap on identity columns - are judged separately, on their own evidence, and are not moved by this decision.

conditions.condition: a verification token is still read from the query string
the request log line still records the path rather than the full URL, so the token is not in this log

decisions.note: Two query parameters carry a credential. The denominator is every query key the application reads, not a sample: lang 7, role 4, to 3, stream 3, limit 3, as 3, token 2, locale 2, format 2, state 1, next 1, flow 1, email 1, connection_limit 1, code 1. Of those, the two token reads are the finding - registration status and Gekta email verification both accept a verification token in the URL. The OAuth authorization code in the gov-id callback is deliberately not counted as the failure: a code in the query is the authorization code flow’s own design, and whether it is handled correctly is V10’s question. Correction to the reasoning first published with this decision: it said the log-masking middleware has no reference to the URL or query string, "so nothing masks these values in the logs they reach". The first half is true, but the inference was misleading - the middleware logs Express req.path, which excludes the query string, so the platform’s own request log never contains the token to begin with. The verdict does not change, because the defect this requirement names is the credential being in the URL at all: from there it reaches browser history, the Referer header on any outbound link, and whatever access log the Caddy edge keeps, which is not under version control and cannot be inspected from here. What would close it is moving the token out of the URL - a one-time link that is exchanged for a POST, or a token carried in a header - and that changes how verification emails work, so it is a product decision rather than a masking fix.

conditions.condition: the application still operates no server-side cache that could hold sensitive data
the framework configuration that would be the other in-repository cache surface is still present and readable

decisions.note: Half of this is measurable and clean, half is not, so no verdict is recorded. Measurable: the application operates no server-side cache. A scan of 3341 source files finds no Nest CacheModule, no cache-manager, no unstable_cache and no next/cache import; Redis is reported as disabled unless REDIS_URL is set and is listed elsewhere as planned rather than deployed. Not measurable: the requirement also covers load balancers and other server components, and the only such component is the Caddy edge, whose configuration is not under version control. Recording a pass on the application half would claim more than was measured, and recording a failure would state something not measured - the same treatment the edge blocker gets in V4, V11 and V12.

decisions.note: This decision previously recorded that Webvisor session recording reached the authenticated cabinet. That was overstated and the correction is recorded here rather than quietly dropped. Measuring what the server actually sends showed exactly one content-security-policy header on every path - the one set by the web middleware, which does not allow the analytics host in script-src - so the third-party script was blocked and the recorder never initialised. What was true is that the snippet with webvisor enabled was emitted into every page including the cabinet, and that a second policy in next.config.js did allow the host, so the safe outcome depended on which header happened to be applied last. The live leak was narrower and real: the noscript fallback is an image, img-src permits https, and a client with JavaScript disabled reported cabinet page URLs to a third party. All three are now closed. Analytics renders only behind a fail-closed allowlist of four public informational paths; anything unrecognised, including every cabinet, staff, Gekta, assistant, login, registration and recovery path, renders nothing at all - no script and no pixel. Session replay is removed rather than reconfigured, because a safe public-only boundary cannot be demonstrated while the public surface includes credential entry and a free-text assistant. The analytics host is gone from next.config.js so the repository states one intention. Verified by request against a running server: the cabinet page carried the snippet and the pixel before and carries neither after. The public-path render is covered by unit test rather than by request, because this development configuration redirects the public paths to the cabinet. What remains on allowlisted public pages is ordinary pageview telemetry on informational pages, which is not the sensitive-data transfer this requirement is about; whether even that is wanted is an owner decision, and the boundary makes it a one-line change either way.

conditions.condition: one module still declares the sensitive-data classification for the platform
the internal logging sink still consumes that classification rather than its own
the outbound telemetry sink still consumes the same one
personal data is still not collected by default on the outbound channel
the test that fails when a class is enforced internally but not outbound is still present
patterns: is driven by the same classification the internal masker uses
redacts every classified field in request headers

decisions.note: Controls are now implemented to one standard across sinks, which is what this requirement asks even while the protection-level document it refers to does not yet exist. The gap recorded when this chapter was assessed was not that the outbound filter was short, but that there were three independent classifications - eight value patterns and eighteen field names in the logging middleware, twelve of its own in the masked logger, five literal key names in the Sentry hook - and the weakest of the three faced outward. One module now declares the classification and both the internal and the outbound sink consume it, so a class cannot be enforced in one place and forgotten in the other. The outbound scrubber reaches every surface an event carries: body, headers, cookies, query string, url, extra, contexts, tags, message, user, breadcrumbs and exception values; the previous hook reached one object at one level. Field names are matched normalized for case and separators but exactly rather than by substring, because substring matching would redact tokenCount and emailVerifiedAt and produce a false sense of coverage. Personal data is no longer collected by SDK default. The tests derive their cases from the classification itself, so adding a class widens the outbound assertions automatically; the surfaces were mutation-checked, and dropping header coverage from the scrubber turns two of them red. What this decision does not claim is that the classification is the right one - that is the owner decision recorded against V14.1.1, and this change makes the platform consistent with whatever that document eventually says rather than substituting for it.

conditions.condition: content-type sniffing is still refused on every response
the framework still sets the same header globally

decisions.note: One half is present, the other is not readable. Content-type handling is controlled: X-Content-Type-Options nosniff is set by the web middleware on every response and again by the framework configuration under a global path rule, so a cached response cannot be reinterpreted as a different type. The other half of this requirement is web-server behaviour - returning 404 or 302 for a path that does not exist, rather than serving a different valid file - and that is decided by the Caddy edge, whose configuration is not under version control. Web cache deception depends on exactly that behaviour, so the requirement cannot be settled from the repository.

conditions.condition: the one measured minimization control still exists
the KYC check still returns a verdict and a bank name rather than the account number it was given

decisions.note: Not assessed, and deliberately not failed. Two real controls were found and are recorded so they are not lost: the AI assistant builds its context through a minimizer that drops any key matching a denial list of eleven sensitive names and caps string length, array length, key count and depth; and the KYC service accepts a bank account number as input and returns only a pass verdict and the bank name, without echoing the account back. What was not done is the measurement this requirement actually needs - reading every response shape for over-return, and comparing each against a definition of what the minimum is for that data class. That definition does not exist (V14.1.1), so even a complete sweep would have no standard to measure against. A failure here would have to name an endpoint that returns more than it should, and none was identified; asserting one on the strength of an absent control elsewhere would be the same error as passing a requirement on a numerator. Log masking is listed only to say it is not an answer to this: masking a value on its way to a log does not reduce what a response returns.

conditions.condition: retention is still implemented for the one data class that has it
retention classification now exists per class, so the gap is enforcement rather than the classification itself
patterns: not-enforced; no automatic deletion or archival job exists

decisions.note: Update: the classification half of this requirement is no longer missing. Every class now carries a documented retention requirement with a named basis - 402-ФЗ Art. 29 where the record is accounting-linked, 152-ФЗ Art. 5(7) otherwise - so the earlier note’s claim that "without the classification there is no way to tell whether that is retention by decision or by default" no longer holds; it is now by decision, stated per class. What remains missing, and is exactly what keeps this FAIL, is the "ensuring that... is deleted automatically" half the requirement also asks for. The schema states enforcement honestly rather than inferring it from the new document: auth-mail (seven-day default, capped at a year) and the EDO webhook purge (twenty-four hours) remain the only two automatic deletion mechanisms in the platform, and every personal-data class - C3 through C7 - is marked not-enforced, because no deletion or archival job exists for deals, documents, audit records or registration data. Documenting a retention window is not the same action as building the job that honours it, and this decision does not conflate the two.

conditions.condition: the application still accepts user-submitted files
nothing in the tree strips metadata from an uploaded file

decisions.note: User-submitted files are accepted and processed, and their metadata is kept. The attachments endpoint takes multipart uploads and runs text extraction over them; nothing at any point removes embedded metadata, and a scan of 3442 source files finds no metadata-stripping call of any kind. Photographs taken in the field - which is what a grain platform receives from an elevator, a laboratory or a driver - routinely carry GPS coordinates, device identifiers and timestamps in EXIF, and those survive into storage unchanged. There is no consent flow that would make retention of that metadata a user choice, because there is no classification saying it is sensitive in the first place.

conditions.condition: no response anywhere asks the browser to clear site data
logout still clears cookies without clearing client storage
authenticated data is still written to client storage that outlives the session

decisions.note: Logging out ends the session but does not clear what the session left behind. The logout route is otherwise careful - it checks CSRF, revokes upstream, clears the authentication cookies and sets no-store - and that is exactly why the gap is worth stating precisely: cookies are handled, client storage is not. No response in 2576 web source files sends Clear-Site-Data, and the logout handler contains no reference to local or session storage. Meanwhile conversation history and project lists from the Gekta assistant, per-deal document lists and checklists from the documents dropzone, and the support profile all persist in localStorage across logout, on a shared or borrowed device as much as a personal one. The requirement also asks for a client-side path that cleans up when the server is unreachable at logout, and none exists.

conditions.condition: the framework anti-caching header is still scoped to the entry paths rather than applied globally
the login, session and finance handlers still set no cache header of their own

decisions.note: Most handlers do this correctly and a minority do not, so both numbers are given. Of 118 route handlers under apps/web/app/api, 86 set Cache-Control no-store, 1 sets a different Cache-Control value for a streaming response, 4 set only a framework directive, and 27 set nothing at all. The 4 are called out separately because they look like coverage and are not: export const dynamic force-dynamic and revalidate 0 govern the Next.js cache, not the browser’s, and neither emits a response header. The framework configuration does not fill the gap either - its no-store block applies to exactly four entry paths, none of them under /api, while the global rule applies security headers that contain no Cache-Control. Among the 27 uncovered handlers are the cabinet login response, the cabinet session endpoint and the whole commercial surface: companies, insurance, finance applications, dispatch, provider assignments, queue, survey, market and expansion.

conditions.condition: a personal-data profile is still written to browser storage
no credential is written to browser storage, which is the part that is right

decisions.note: The exception this requirement allows is session tokens, and the data stored is not that. The support widget writes a profile containing the user’s name, their phone number or email address, and their organization into sessionStorage and localStorage both, under three key names. The Gekta assistant persists whole conversations and project lists, and the documents dropzone persists per-deal document lists and checklists - commercial content about identifiable counterparties, on the client, indefinitely. What the platform does get right is credited and machine-checked: no token, JWT or password is written to browser storage anywhere in 2576 web source files, so the classic version of this failure is absent. Without a data classification (V14.1.1) there is no rule that would have told a component author the support profile was not theirs to persist.

conditions.condition: logging is implemented and would be what an inventory has to describe
no inventory documents the logging performed at each layer

decisions.note: Logging is implemented across three channels and none of it is inventoried. This is the fourth chapter to fail on the same missing artefact, after V2, V7 and V8: the rules the controls implement are written nowhere, so a strong implementation cannot be reviewed against an intent. Worth treating as one systemic gap rather than four unrelated ones.

conditions.condition: the audit channel carries who, where and what
the HTTP channel carries method, path, status, actor and address

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment deliberately not claimed, and the reason is a denominator. The requirement says EACH log entry. Two of the three channels are good: the auth audit carries userId, sessionId, membershipId, organizationId, tenantId, action, outcome and reason, and the HTTP request line carries method, path, status, duration, masked address and actor. The third channel is 45 Nest Logger instances writing free text plus 5 raw console calls, and those will not all carry who and where. Claiming a chapter-wide PASS from the two structured channels would repeat the mistake corrected under V2.2.1, where a real control was measured against the wrong denominator.

conditions.condition: the production host is still a single REG.RU virtual server
and its configuration is still managed on the host

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment blocked on host configuration the repository cannot show, the same blocker recorded under V12 and V4. There is no NTP, chrony or timesyncd evidence anywhere, because clock synchronisation is a property of the host rather than of this codebase. Credited without letting it answer the question: the audit chain deliberately provides a total order that does not depend on wall-clock ties, so correlating audit events does not rest on synchronised clocks - but the requirement asks that the time sources be synchronised, and that remains unverified.

conditions.condition: logs are broadcast to a named external destination
no document defines the destinations logs may be sent to

decisions.note: The requirement is that logs go only to documented destinations. The destinations are knowable - the collector forwards to Loki - but nothing documents them, so there is no stated set for the actual behaviour to be inside of. The gap is the documentation, not the routing.

conditions.condition: the production host is still a single REG.RU virtual server
and its configuration is still managed on the host

decisions.note: Applicability decided; assessment not claimed. A log processor exists and the collector is configured to feed it, which is the shape the requirement wants. But the application emits free-text lines rather than a common structured format, and whether Loki parses them usefully is a property of the deployed pipeline rather than of this repository. Asserting a PASS would claim something about a system this programme cannot observe.

conditions.condition: sensitive values are masked before they reach a log line
the masking middleware is applied to every route

decisions.note: Logging is enforced according to the data protection level rather than left to each call site. The middleware masks Russian INN, OGRN, BIK, bank account, phone, email, card number and passport patterns, masks addresses, replaces declared sensitive body fields outright, and recurses into nested objects. It is applied globally via forRoutes(*), so a new route inherits it rather than having to remember it.

conditions.condition: the audit record can express a failed attempt, not only a successful one
and carries the subject and reason of the attempt

decisions.note: Both halves of the requirement are met, and the second half is the one usually missing. The audit event type carries an outcome of SUCCESS, FAILURE or DENIED, and those are not decorative: the tree writes 83 SUCCESS, 22 DENIED and 6 FAILURE across 21 call sites outside the audit module. Login, logout, MFA verification, MFA step-up start and verify, email verification and membership selection are all recorded.

conditions.condition: a denied authorization decision is representable and recorded

decisions.note: Failed authorization attempts are logged: DENIED is a first-class outcome in the audit schema and is written at 22 sites. Stated with its limit - the L3 half of this requirement asks for all authorization decisions including successful ones, and what is recorded is the auth-module decisions rather than every authorization check in the application. The requirement is met at L2 and this note does not claim more.

conditions.condition: the anti-automation guard exists and can log
no document defines which security events must be logged

decisions.note: The requirement has two halves and both fail, for different reasons. The first asks that the application log the security events DEFINED IN THE DOCUMENTATION - and no document defines any, the same missing artefact recorded under V16.1.1, so there is no defined set to log. The second asks that attempts to bypass security controls be logged, and they largely are not: the rate-limit guard logs only when its own enforcement fails, not when it rejects a caller, so an anti-automation trip leaves no record beyond the request line; and the validation pipe is installed without an exceptionFactory, so a rejected payload produces a 400 and no security event. Credited: authentication and authorization bypass attempts ARE recorded, as DENIED and FAILURE outcomes under V16.3.1 and V16.3.2. The gap is the input-validation and anti-automation controls named by this requirement, not the auth ones.

conditions.condition: a failure outcome with a reason is recordable
the request channel logs every response including failures

decisions.note: Unexpected errors and control failures are recorded. The audit channel carries FAILURE with a reason, 44 logger.error or logger.warn sites cover unexpected conditions, and the request middleware logs every response with its status code, so a failing request is visible even when no handler logs it explicitly.

conditions.condition: an attacker-controlled header is interpolated into a log line
and nothing encodes or strips control characters

decisions.note: Masking is not encoding, and this requirement asks for encoding. The middleware interpolates the User-Agent - a request header the caller controls - directly into a logged template string, and nothing anywhere strips or encodes newlines or control characters. A newline in that header produces a forged additional log line. Credited so this is not read as an absence of log hygiene: the PII masking assessed under V16.2.5 is real and thorough. These are two different controls and only one is present.

conditions.condition: the audit chain is enforced by database constraints rather than convention

decisions.note: Logs cannot be modified, and the guarantee is structural. The auth audit table carries a generated chain key and an explicit chain sequence, with unique indexes turning three invariants into constraints PostgreSQL enforces: one event per position, no repeated hash, at most one child per parent. Append-only enforcement sits on top of that. Worth noting deliberately: append-only was the wrong control when it appeared under the tenancy requirement V8.4.1, and it is exactly the right one here - the distinction was made rather than assumed.

conditions.condition: logs are pushed to a separate system over a plaintext endpoint

decisions.note: A logically separate system exists and logs are shipped to it, which is the structural half of the requirement. The transport is not secure: the collector pushes to Loki over plaintext http. Unlike the edge requirements recorded as unassessed, this is a FAIL rather than a blocked assessment, and the distinction matters - those depend on a configuration held outside the repository, whereas this configuration IS in the repository and requires a plaintext endpoint. Same finding as V12.3.1 seen from the logging side, not a second discovery.

conditions.condition: the service entry point installs the pipeline that shapes error responses

decisions.note: Measured both ways, because a numerator alone would not settle it. 284 exceptions are thrown as structured payloads carrying a stable machine code, and zero exceptions anywhere are constructed from a caught error object - so no site passes an internal message through to the consumer. An uncaught throw is turned into a generic 500 by the framework default without a stack. The zero is what makes this a PASS; the 284 only shows the convention is consistent.

conditions.condition: no authorization decision falls back to an empty or permissive result

decisions.note: Stated as what was scanned rather than what was counted. The application has 93 sites that degrade to an empty or null result when an external read fails, which on its own proves nothing - that same pattern is how a failed authorization lookup becomes an empty allow list. Every one of those sites was checked against paths named for auth, permission, capability, role, access, guard, policy or membership, and none of them sits on a security decision: the fallbacks are read-side projections. The application degrades without opening.

conditions.condition: the framework converts an unhandled route exception into a controlled response
and a failure outcome is recordable when it happens

decisions.note: An exception inside a request does not leave the application in an open state: the framework converts it into an error response, the transaction wrapper rolls back rather than committing partial work, and the session and authorization checks that would have run are not skipped by the failure - they precede it. Scoped deliberately: this covers failure inside a request. Failure outside one is the subject of V16.5.4, which does not pass.

conditions.condition: the worker process installs last-resort handlers
the API process installs neither those nor a global exception filter

decisions.note: The two processes are not held to the same standard, and the requirement asks about the last resort. The outbox worker installs process-level uncaughtException and unhandledRejection handlers that log and shut down deliberately. The API installs neither, and registers no global exception filter, so it relies on the framework default - which does catch exceptions thrown inside a route handler, and that is credited under V16.5.3. It does not catch an exception thrown outside a request context, which is precisely what a last-resort handler is for. The worker being covered does not answer for the API.
